posts.title: About 25 minutes a night
posts.insight: In short trials in people aged 60 and over, sleeping tablets added about 25 minutes of self-reported sleep a night, while memory problems, confusion and daytime tiredness were more common than with a dummy pill.
posts.angle: Put the benefit in minutes beside the harms so the person can weigh them. Position: CBT for insomnia first; a short course of a tablet can still be a reasonable choice after discussion.
posts.position_basis: mixed: the minutes, the 1 in 13 and 1 in 6 figures and the guideline order are empirical or guideline statements; 'weigh it with the person' is clinical interpretation

captions.x:
Sleeping tablets in people aged 60 and over: about 25 extra minutes of sleep a night, on average.

That comes from a meta-analysis of short trials (5 nights to 9 weeks), with sleep reported by the people taking them.

In those trials, for every 13 people who took a tablet, about 1 more slept better than with a dummy pill. For every 6, about 1 more had a side effect. Memory problems, confusion and daytime tiredness were more common with the tablets.

European and US guidelines put CBT for insomnia first. A short course of a tablet can still be discussed if that is not enough.
captions.linkedin:
Sleeping tablets in people aged 60 and over add about 25 minutes of sleep a night, on average.

That figure comes from a meta-analysis of 24 randomised trials (Glass and colleagues, BMJ 2005). The trials were short, from 5 nights to 9 weeks, and sleep was reported by the people taking the tablets. They also woke about once less every two nights.

The harms were measured in the same trials. Memory problems, confusion and daytime tiredness were more common with the tablets than with a dummy pill.

The authors gave a rough guide. For every 13 people who took a tablet, about 1 more reported better sleep. For every 6, about 1 more had a side effect, most often drowsiness, headache, nightmares or stomach upset. These two figures come from different sets of trials, and the 1 in 13 is imprecise: it could be anywhere from about 1 in 7 to 1 in 63.

Allowing for unpublished negative trials, the authors' adjusted estimate of the gain was about 15 minutes.

The American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria advise avoiding benzodiazepines and Z-drugs in people aged 65 and over, noting falls, fractures and confusion.

European and American guidelines recommend CBT for insomnia (a structured talking and sleep-scheduling treatment) as the first treatment for long-term insomnia. If it is not enough, a short course of a tablet can be discussed.

Put the minutes and the harms side by side with the person. Some will still choose a short course; that choice should be made with the numbers in view.
captions.bluesky:
In short trials in people over 60, sleeping tablets added about 25 minutes of sleep a night.

Memory problems, confusion and daytime tiredness were more common than with a dummy pill.

Guidelines put CBT for insomnia first. Weigh the minutes against the harms before starting.

posts.title: Acting out dreams
posts.insight: Dream enactment in later life can be REM sleep behaviour disorder, which in specialist-centre cohorts was followed by Parkinson's disease or dementia with Lewy bodies in about 6 in 100 a year. A report of dream enactment is a reason to assess, not a diagnosis.
posts.angle: Take the history from the bed partner, make the bedroom safe, review medicines without ending the assessment there, and have an honest conversation about uncertainty.
posts.position_basis: mixed: conversion rates, DLB core feature, population prevalence and bedroom safety advice are empirical or guideline; the duty to discuss risk carefully is ethical judgement

captions.x:
Punching, kicking or shouting during a dream, in a person over 60, is worth a proper history from the bed partner.

It can be REM sleep behaviour disorder. In 1,280 people with the diagnosis confirmed on a sleep study, about 6 in 100 a year developed Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies or a related condition; about 3 in 4 by 12 years.

Those were specialist-centre patients. In a Swiss population study, 368 of about 2,000 adults reported acting out dreams, and 21 had the disorder on testing.

So: assess, make the bedroom safe, review medicines, and be open about the uncertainty.
captions.linkedin:
Punching, kicking or shouting during a dream, in a person over 60, is worth a proper history from the bed partner.

It can be REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD). It is one of the four core clinical features of dementia with Lewy bodies, and it often starts years before other symptoms (McKeith 2017).

In 1,280 people with sleep-study-confirmed RBD at 24 specialist centres, about 6 in 100 a year developed Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies or multiple system atrophy. The 12-year estimate was about 3 in 4 (Postuma 2019). Most were men, and average follow-up was 4.6 years.

That is not a prognosis for everyone who acts out dreams. In a Swiss population study, 368 of about 2,000 adults reported dream enactment; only 21 had RBD on a sleep study.

A practical sequence:

1. Ask the bed partner about chasing or attacking dream themes and injuries from movement in sleep.
2. Think of mimics, including severe sleep apnoea, and refer for a sleep study if there is doubt.
3. Make the bedroom safe: remove objects that could hurt, pad sharp furniture and the headboard, put a mat beside the bed, and sleep apart if episodes are severe.
4. Review medicines. Some antidepressants are linked with dream enactment, but people whose symptoms came with antidepressants still showed early signs of Parkinson-type disease in one cohort. A medicines review should not end the assessment.

We should also make time to discuss what the diagnosis may mean. Patients and professionals both see that conversation as essential, and it needs honesty about uncertainty and follow-up.
captions.bluesky:
Acting out dreams in later life can be REM sleep behaviour disorder. In confirmed cases, about 6 in 100 a year went on to Parkinson's or Lewy body dementia.

Most people who report dream enactment do not have it. Ask the bed partner, make the bedroom safe, refer if in doubt.

posts.title: The booklet that changed the decision
posts.insight: In a Quebec trial, older people given a booklet on benzodiazepine risks and a plan for cutting down were more likely to have stopped at 6 months: about 27 in 100 against 5 in 100 with usual care. Most raised it with their doctor or pharmacist themselves.
posts.angle: Treat the person taking the tablet as the decision-maker, inside a pharmacy system that follows through. Ask your pharmacist for written information and a slow, agreed plan.
posts.position_basis: mixed: trial results are empirical; treating the person as decision-maker is ethical judgement

captions.x:
Older people who had taken benzodiazepines for years were handed a booklet, and many stopped. You can ask your pharmacist for written information on the risks and a slow plan for cutting down.

In a Quebec trial of 303 people aged 65 to 95, those given such a booklet were more likely to have stopped at 6 months: about 27 in 100, against 5 in 100 with usual care. About 62 in 100 raised it with their doctor or pharmacist themselves.

Local pharmacies ran it. Posting information alone did not reduce use in a large US trial.

Cutting down can bring withdrawal symptoms, so go slowly with a plan.
captions.linkedin:
Older people who had taken benzodiazepines for years were handed a booklet, and many stopped.

If you have taken a sleeping tablet or a benzodiazepine for years, you can ask your pharmacist for two things: written information on the risks, and a slow plan for cutting down.

In a Quebec trial, 303 people aged 65 to 95 who had taken benzodiazepines long term were given a booklet on the risks with a written tapering plan. Six months later, about 27 in 100 had stopped, against about 5 in 100 with usual care. A further 11 in 100 had cut their dose.

About 62 in 100 of those who got the booklet raised stopping with their doctor or pharmacist themselves. The person taking the tablet started the conversation.

A second Quebec trial added a message from the pharmacist to the doctor. Among people on sleeping tablets or similar sedatives, 43 in 100 had stopped at 6 months, against 9 in 100 with usual care.

Two cautions. Both trials ran through community pharmacies, and the researchers say the results need testing elsewhere; in a large US trial, mailing information to people with dementia and their prescribers did not reduce use. And cutting down can be uncomfortable: 29 of 77 people who tried to taper reported withdrawal symptoms, though none needed hospital care.

We should give older people this information directly and treat them as the people making the decision. Then support a slow, agreed plan.

posts.title: Hearing aids out, smoke alarm on
posts.insight: In a sleep laboratory study of adults with hearing loss, a standard high-pitched smoke alarm woke about 56 in 100 from deep sleep, a vibrating pad about 80 to 84 in 100, and a flashing strobe about 27 in 100.
posts.angle: If you take your hearing aids out at night, check which alarm would wake you, and ask your fire and rescue service for a home fire safety visit.
posts.position_basis: empirical finding for the waking rates; practical advice is clinical interpretation

captions.x:
If you take your hearing aids out at night, would your smoke alarm wake you?

In a sleep laboratory study of 38 adults aged 18 to 80 with hearing loss, a standard high-pitched alarm woke about 56 in 100 from deep sleep. A vibrating pad under the pillow or mattress woke about 80 to 84 in 100. A flashing strobe light woke about 27 in 100.

It was a small study, in a laboratory.

Fire and rescue services in the UK carry out home fire safety visits. Ask for one, say you are hard of hearing, and ask whether they can fit an alarm with a vibrating pad.
captions.linkedin:
If you take your hearing aids out at night, would your smoke alarm wake you?

An Australian sleep laboratory study tested this in 38 adults aged 18 to 80 with mild to moderately severe hearing loss, woken from deep sleep (Bruck and Thomas, 2009).

A standard high-pitched smoke alarm woke about 56 in 100 of them.

A lower-pitched alarm sound at the same loudness woke about 92 in 100.

A vibrating pad under the pillow or mattress woke about 80 to 84 in 100.

A flashing strobe light woke about 27 in 100, even when it was brighter than the US standard.

This was a small laboratory study of adults of all ages, not only older people, and it tested deep sleep only. It still gives a clear message: a flashing light on its own is a poor way to wake someone.

Fire and rescue services in the UK carry out home fire safety visits, and in England every service offers them. You can ask for one for yourself or a relative. Say that the person is hard of hearing and takes hearing aids out at night. Ask whether they can fit an alarm with a vibrating pad, and check that any kit you are offered includes one and not only a flashing light.
captions.bluesky:
Hearing aids out at night? In a lab study of adults with hearing loss, a standard smoke alarm woke about 56 in 100 from deep sleep. A vibrating pad woke about 80 in 100; a flashing light, 27 in 100.

Ask your fire service for a home safety visit.

posts.title: The sleep hygiene booklet was the comparison
posts.insight: Sleep hygiene advice alone is weak treatment for long-term insomnia. In trials, it was what the comparison group got; brief nurse-delivered behavioural treatment did better.
posts.angle: A leaflet about caffeine and dark bedrooms is a start, not the treatment. Offer sleep restriction, stimulus control or full CBT for insomnia.
posts.position_basis: mixed: trial and guideline statements are empirical; 'do not stop at the leaflet' is clinical interpretation

captions.x:
In the English HABIT trial, the sleep hygiene booklet was what the comparison group received.

People who also had four sessions of sleep restriction therapy from a practice nurse had less severe insomnia at 6 months: average 10.9 against 13.9 on a 0 to 28 scale. Mean age was 55, so not an older-adult trial.

In 79 older adults (average age 72), about 2 in 3 improved with two nurse sessions and two calls of behavioural treatment, against 1 in 4 with printed information.

The AASM advises against sleep hygiene alone for long-term insomnia. Offer the active parts.

More Teaching round posts take one clinical shortcut at a time and qualify it.
captions.linkedin:
In the English HABIT trial, the sleep hygiene booklet was what the comparison group received.

The trial ran in 35 general practices. People who also had four sessions of sleep restriction therapy from a practice nurse had less severe insomnia at 6 months: an average score of 10.9 against 13.9 on the 0 to 28 Insomnia Severity Index. The treatment was likely to be good value for the NHS. It was open label, with a self-reported outcome, and the mean age was 55 (range 19 to 88).

For older adults specifically, a US trial of 79 people (average age 72) with long-term insomnia tested two nurse sessions and two phone calls of brief behavioural treatment. About 2 in 3 improved, against 1 in 4 given printed information, and the benefit lasted to 6 months. It was small and single-centre.

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine suggests not using sleep hygiene as a single treatment for long-term insomnia (a conditional recommendation). It strongly recommends multicomponent CBT for insomnia, and suggests stimulus control, sleep restriction or relaxation as single treatments.

Sleep hygiene can stay inside a fuller treatment. It should not be the whole response.

In practice:

1. Use the leaflet as a starting point.
2. Offer sleep restriction or stimulus control, or refer for full CBT for insomnia.
3. Review with a sleep diary.

More Teaching round posts take one clinical shortcut at a time and qualify it.

posts.title: Restless legs: iron and the medicines list first
posts.insight: Before adding a drug for restless legs, check ferritin and transferrin saturation and look for aggravating medicines; the 2025 AASM guideline advises against dopamine agonists as standard because of augmentation.
posts.angle: Iron and the medicines list come first; gabapentinoids carry falls-related cautions in older people.
posts.position_basis: mixed: guideline content is empirical/guideline; applying it to older people with falls is clinical interpretation

captions.x:
Restless legs in an older person: check iron and the medicines list before adding a drug.

The 2025 US AASM guideline advises ferritin and transferrin saturation in everyone with troublesome symptoms, and iron if ferritin is 75 or below or saturation under 20%. Those cut-offs are expert consensus.

Look for aggravators: alcohol, caffeine, sedating antihistamines, serotonergic antidepressants, dopamine blockers, untreated sleep apnoea.

The guideline now advises against pramipexole, ropinirole or rotigotine as standard, because of augmentation. Gabapentinoids come first, but weigh sleepiness and dizziness in someone who has fallen.
captions.linkedin:
Restless legs in an older person: check iron and the medicines list before adding a drug.

The 2025 US guideline from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine made four changes worth knowing.

1. Iron studies for everyone with clinically significant restless legs: ferritin and transferrin saturation, ideally in the morning and off iron for 24 hours. Offer iron if ferritin is 75 or below (ng/mL, the same number in micrograms per litre) or saturation is under 20%. The guideline says these cut-offs come from expert consensus and have not been tested directly.

2. A ferritin that is normal by the usual standard can still be low enough for iron to help in restless legs.

3. Look for aggravators before adding anything: alcohol, caffeine, sedating antihistamines, serotonergic antidepressants, medicines that block dopamine such as some anti-sickness drugs and antipsychotics, and untreated sleep apnoea.

4. Gabapentin and pregabalin now come first among medicines. The guideline advises against pramipexole, ropinirole and rotigotine as standard treatment, because of augmentation: over months to years, symptoms start earlier in the day, come on faster and spread. That recommendation is conditional.

In older people, gabapentinoids commonly cause sleepiness and dizziness. The Beers Criteria advise lower doses with reduced kidney function, and avoiding them with opioids or with two or more other drugs acting on the brain, because of falls and fractures.

For someone who has already fallen, that trade-off needs discussing before the first prescription.
captions.bluesky:
Restless legs: a 2025 US guideline advises checking ferritin and transferrin saturation in everyone, and reviewing aggravating drugs first.

It now advises against dopamine agonists as standard because symptoms can worsen over time. Weigh gabapentinoid falls risk.

posts.title: Treating insomnia and later depression
posts.insight: In one trial of 291 people aged 60 and over with insomnia, CBT for insomnia was followed by about half the risk of major depression over up to 3 years compared with sleep education.
posts.angle: Promising, from one trial, with uneven drop-out. Reason to treat insomnia properly, not proof it prevents depression in everyone.
posts.position_basis: empirical finding for the result and limitations; clinical interpretation for 'treat insomnia properly'

captions.x:
Can treating insomnia in later life lower the chance of depression?

One Los Angeles trial tested it in 291 people aged 60 and over with insomnia but no depression. Over up to 3 years, 12 in 100 given CBT for insomnia developed major depression, against 26 in 100 given sleep education. The risk over time was about half.

Read it with care: one site, more than 8 in 10 participants White, and more drop-out in the CBT group (73 in 100 completed 2 years, against 87 in 100).

Promising, from one trial. It is one more reason to offer CBT for insomnia properly.
captions.linkedin:
Can treating insomnia in later life lower the chance of depression?

Irwin and colleagues (JAMA Psychiatry 2022) randomised 291 people aged 60 and over (average age 70) who had insomnia but were not depressed. They had 2 months of either CBT for insomnia (a structured talking and sleep-scheduling treatment) or sleep education.

Over up to 3 years, 19 of 156 people in the CBT group (12 in 100) developed major depression, against 35 of 135 in the sleep education group (26 in 100). Those are crude proportions of everyone randomised. The main analysis, which allows for time in the study, found the risk over time was about half as high with CBT; the true reduction could be smaller or larger.

Read it with care.

It was one trial, at one site.

More than 8 in 10 participants were White, and people with a major health event in the past year were excluded, so frailer older people are under-represented.

More people dropped out of follow-up in the CBT group: 73 in 100 completed 2 years, against 87 in 100 with sleep education. Only just over half completed 3 years. Uneven drop-out could bias the result either way.

This is a promising finding that needs repeating. It does not need to be proved before we act on the insomnia itself, which already has good evidence for CBT as first treatment.

In one trial of 291 people over 60 with insomnia, 12 in 100 given CBT for insomnia developed major depression over up to 3 years, against 26 in 100 given sleep education.

One site, and more drop-out in the CBT group. Promising, not settled.

Promising and worth repeating. Meanwhile, insomnia itself deserves proper treatment.

posts.title: Your CPAP machine goes to hospital with you
posts.insight: If you use CPAP for sleep apnoea, specialist guidance advises continuing it in hospital around surgery, and hospitals may ask you to bring your own.
posts.angle: Pack the machine, mask, tubing and power lead, and tell staff. For unplanned admissions, ask someone to bring it in.
posts.position_basis: mixed: surgical guidance is a guideline statement; extending it to unplanned admissions is practical advice

captions.x:
Pack your CPAP machine if you use one for sleep apnoea and are going into hospital. Take all of it: machine, mask, tubing and power lead.

Anaesthesia and sleep specialists advise continuing CPAP around an operation, before and after. Hospitals should have a machine or ask you to bring your own.

Strong painkillers and some sedatives may make breathing problems more likely in people with sleep apnoea, though the evidence is limited.

Tell staff you use CPAP. If you are admitted unexpectedly, ask someone to bring it in, and ask whether the ward needs to check it.
captions.linkedin:
Pack your CPAP machine if you use one for sleep apnoea and are going into hospital. Take all of it: the machine, the mask, the tubing and the power lead.

Sleep apnoea means breathing stops and starts during sleep. CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) blows air through a mask to keep the airway open.

The Society of Anesthesia and Sleep Medicine advises that people who use CPAP keep using it in hospital around an operation, before and after. It says hospitals should either have a machine available or ask patients to bring their own. This guidance is North American and written for planned surgery.

A second guideline from the same society notes that strong painkillers such as morphine-type drugs, and some sedatives, may make breathing problems more likely in people with sleep apnoea. The evidence for this is limited. CPAP does not replace proper monitoring.

What you can do:

Tell the pre-operative team and the ward that you use CPAP.

Take the whole kit with you.

If you are admitted unexpectedly, ask a relative or friend to bring it in.

Ask whether the ward needs to check your machine before you use it. Local policies differ, and settings may need adjusting after surgery.

posts.title: Melatonin: realistic expectations
posts.insight: Melatonin helps people fall asleep about 7 minutes sooner on average; in Alzheimer's disease it may make little or no difference; and supplements tested in North America often did not match the label.
posts.angle: Set realistic expectations and agree in advance what counts as success and when to stop.
posts.position_basis: mixed: effect sizes and product testing are empirical; 'decide success and a stop date' is clinical interpretation

captions.x:
Thinking of trying melatonin for sleep? Decide first what would count as success.

In trials of people with insomnia and other sleep problems, melatonin helped people fall asleep about 7 minutes sooner and sleep about 8 minutes longer than a dummy pill, on average.

In people with Alzheimer's disease, it may make little or no difference to sleep. Other options had some evidence there.

When supplements sold in the US were tested, 22 of 25 gummy products were wrongly labelled.

The European insomnia guideline supports prescribed slow-release melatonin for up to 3 months from age 55. Agree a date to stop if it has not helped.
captions.linkedin:
Thinking of trying melatonin for sleep? Decide first what would count as success.

Melatonin is a hormone the body makes in the evening. It is sold as a supplement in many countries and prescribed as a slow-release tablet.

What it does, on average: in trials of people with insomnia and other sleep problems, it helped people fall asleep about 7 minutes sooner and sleep about 8 minutes longer than a dummy pill. Those trials included people of all ages.

In dementia: a Cochrane review found that in people with Alzheimer's disease and poor sleep, melatonin up to 10 mg may make little or no difference over 8 to 10 weeks. The evidence is limited. No serious side effects were reported. The same review found some evidence for other medicines, so this does not mean nothing helps.

What is in the bottle: when supplements sold in the US and Canada were tested, most did not match the label. In one US study, 22 of 25 gummy products bought online were wrongly labelled, from about three quarters to more than three times the stated dose; one contained none. These were North American products, not prescribed tablets.

What the guideline says: the European insomnia guideline supports prescribed slow-release melatonin for up to 3 months in people aged 55 and over with insomnia. It does not recommend ordinary fast-release melatonin for insomnia.

If you try it, agree two things at the start with your doctor or pharmacist: what would count as success, and when you will stop if it has not helped.

posts.title: Ask a care home about the night
posts.insight: Night checks, continence care, noise and light can all wake care home residents; tailoring checks to each person's skin risk reduced waking without harming skin in US studies.
posts.angle: Four questions families and residents can ask to learn the home's plan for nights, respectful of night staff.
posts.position_basis: mixed: study findings are empirical; the bedtime question is a values judgement about choice

captions.x:
Choosing or reviewing a care home? Ask about the night, not only the day.

In US nursing home studies, routine night checks, with their light and noise, were linked with residents waking. Being wet rarely woke them. Setting checks by each person's skin risk cut waking with no harm to skin.

Four questions: How are night checks planned for each person? How is continence care done if someone is asleep? How are noise and light kept down? What time do residents go to bed, and who decides?

Some checks are needed. The studies are small, old and American, and UK staff report too few night staff.
captions.linkedin:
Choosing or reviewing a care home? Ask about the night, not only the day.

In four US nursing homes, about 7 in 10 residents screened for a sleep study (339 of 492) were asleep in at least 15 in 100 daytime checks. Broken nights are part of that.

Older US studies found that being wet rarely woke residents: about 4 in 100 night-time awakenings were linked to a wet episode. The light and noise of routine continence checks were linked with waking. When checks were set by each person's skin risk, every 2 or 4 hours, and care was given when people were already awake, care-related waking fell with no harm to skin.

In UK interviews, care home staff describe settling residents into dark, quiet rooms, and say there are too few night staff to help residents who wake.

Four questions to ask:

1. How are night checks planned for each person, and can they be changed?
2. How is continence care done at night if someone is asleep?
3. How are noise and lights kept down, and what happens if someone is awake at 3am?
4. What time do residents go to bed, and who decides?

Some checks are needed for skin and safety. The evidence is small, mostly old and American. These questions ask the home to explain its plan; a good plan also needs enough night staff.

posts.title: CBT for insomnia down the phone
posts.insight: The recommended first treatment for long-term insomnia is CBT, and phone sessions worked in older adults: a year later 56 in 100 had no significant insomnia, against 26 in 100 given information only.
posts.angle: Routes that need the internet miss many older people; ask for CBT for insomnia by phone or in person.
posts.position_basis: mixed: trial and survey figures are empirical; that services should offer non-internet routes is ethical judgement

captions.x:
About 1 in 5 people aged 60 and over living at home in England did not use the internet at all in 2020.

Any route to insomnia treatment that needs the internet will miss them.

A US trial offers another route. 327 people aged 60 and over with insomnia and arthritis pain had six phone sessions of CBT for insomnia. A year later, 56 in 100 had no significant insomnia, against 26 in 100 given information only.

If you have long-term insomnia, ask your GP practice: can I have CBT for insomnia by phone or in person?
captions.linkedin:
About 1 in 5 people aged 60 and over living in their own homes in England did not use the internet at all in 2020. Daily use was lowest in the oldest age groups, in more deprived areas and among lonelier people. The real figure is probably higher, because care home residents were not included.

CBT for insomnia (a structured talking and sleep-scheduling treatment) is recommended as the first treatment for long-term insomnia by US guidelines. Any route to it that needs the internet will miss many of these people.

A US trial tested a route that does not. 327 people aged 60 and over, all with insomnia and osteoarthritis pain, had six phone sessions of CBT for insomnia, 20 to 30 minutes each over 8 weeks. The comparison group got information about sleep and arthritis.

A year later, 56 in 100 in the phone group had no clinically significant insomnia, against 26 in 100 in the information group.

The trial did not compare phone with app-based treatment, and everyone in it had arthritis pain. It shows that the phone works.

An English trial also showed that practice nurses can deliver sleep restriction therapy, a core part of CBT for insomnia, in four sessions in general practice.

We should make sure people who are offline are offered a way in. If you have long-term insomnia, ask your GP practice: can I have CBT for insomnia by phone or in person?
captions.bluesky:
About 1 in 5 people over 60 in England did not use the internet in 2020.

In a US trial, phone CBT for insomnia left 56 in 100 older adults free of significant insomnia a year later, against 26 in 100 given information.

Ask for it by phone or in person.

posts.title: The 2am sleep call: two lists
posts.insight: When an older inpatient is awake at night, check pain, bladder, noise and equipment first; next day, review dose times of steroids, donepezil and diuretics.
posts.angle: A sedative adds little sleep and brings harms; the causes patients report and the drug chart times come first.
posts.position_basis: mixed: survey and meta-analysis are empirical; dosing-time advice is expert guidance; the order of actions is clinical interpretation

captions.x:
Called at 2am about an older patient who is wide awake? Two lists.

Tonight: ask about pain, a full bladder, noise and equipment. In 39 Dutch hospitals, those were the disturbances patients reported most, and they slept 83 minutes less than at home. In people over 60, sleeping tablets added only about 25 minutes, with more confusion and daytime tiredness.

Tomorrow, for the day team: is a steroid given after the morning? Is donepezil given at night in someone with sleeplessness or vivid dreams? Is a diuretic given in the evening?
captions.linkedin:
Called at 2am about an older patient who is wide awake? Work through two lists.

Tonight

Ask about pain, a full bladder, noise and equipment. In a survey of 2,005 adults in 39 Dutch hospitals (median age 68), patients reported sleeping 83 minutes less than at home. Noise from other patients, medical equipment, pain and needing the toilet were the disturbances they reported most. These are reported disturbers, not established causes for any one patient.

Before reaching for a sedative: in trials in people over 60, sleeping tablets added only about 25 minutes of sleep, and memory problems, confusion and daytime tiredness were more common than with a dummy pill. Those trials tested nightly use, not a single dose on a ward.

Tomorrow, for the day team

1. Steroids. Prednisolone and similar can disturb sleep. Expert guidance favours a single morning dose where possible. Check whether an evening dose is needed.

2. Donepezil. It can cause sleeplessness and vivid dreams, and reviews suggest morning dosing may help. The evidence is reviews and a small case series.

3. Diuretics. Guidance on night-time urination advises taking them no later than mid to late afternoon. Look for an evening or bedtime dose.

Moving a dose is a day-team decision with the prescriber, not a 2am change.

Next day, check dose times: an evening steroid, night-time donepezil, an evening diuretic.
